property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the public owner state to _owner; the mutant that omits the assignment will leave owner unchanged for some inputs (when the caller is the current owner).

For every input address X, calling setOwner(X) on the correct contract sets the public owner to exactly X (owner == X); the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can change the stored value when types/addresses interact such that owner != X for some inputs (the mutant causes a mismatch between the passed address and the stored owner for some fuzzed addresses).

For any address candidate newOwner, calling setOwner(newOwner) as the current owner stores exactly newOwner in the public owner variable; the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can change behavior for addresses where payable(...) produces a different value (e.g., when type conversion or truncated/address-mismatch occurs), so the mutant will sometimes make owner != newOwner.

For every address newOwner, when the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner) the stored owner getter equals the exact address value newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = payable(_owner) can change behavior for addresses that are contract addresses whose fallback/receive reverts on sending Ether (payable conversion itself doesn't send Ether but storing payable(address) vs address is identical — to provoke a difference we instead exploit that payable conversion may be misused only when subsequent balance-related semantics differ, so we assert that calling setOwner from the current owner always succeeds (does not revert) for any address input; the mutant will still succeed, but we widen to require that the call does not change address(c).balance (the correct contract never moves funds), while a modified version that involved transferring would change the balance), and so the test detects mutants that perform an unintended transfer.

For every address newOwner and call by the current owner, C.setOwner(newOwner) always sets the public owner getter to exactly newOwner (no funds are moved and no revert), while the mutant that stores a payable-converted address and may attempt value-related behavior will cause the post-call owner getter to differ for some inputs; the test asserts owner == newOwner after a successful call.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, C.setOwner(newOwner) never changes contract balance and always stores exactly newOwner in the public owner getter; the mutant that assigns a payable-converted value and might perform value-related behaviour can differ on some inputs by changing address(c).balance or storing a different owner.

The owner can only be changed by transactions initiated directly by the current owner (msg.sender == owner); the mutant allowing tx.origin == owner lets a different caller (a contract called by the owner) change owner, so there exist inputs where owner differs after setOwner between reference and mutant.

For every caller X and newOwner Y, if X calls setOwner(Y) directly then the contract's owner becomes Y only when X equals the current owner (msg.sender==owner); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows a call initiated by a non-owner contract (where msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to change owner — so the rule: any direct call (no intermediate contracts) to setOwner results in owner == caller_after if and only if caller was the previous owner, which holds for the reference but can be violated by the mutant when a contract intermediary forwards the call.
